newsitem.title: USA: INSTANT VIEW - U.S. Fed hikes funds rate 25 bps.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - U.S. Fed hikes funds rate 25 bps.

text.p: Following are comments from U.S. experts after the Federal Reserve raised the federal funds rate by 25 basis points on Tuesday.
The Fed was widely expected to ratchet up the key overnight bank lending rate. In a Reuters survey of 48 economists, 34 predicted a rate hike at Tuesday's meeting.
STEPHEN AXILROD, CONSULTANT, MFR INC, AND FORMER FED BOARD STAFF DIRECTOR: "It's not necessarily or even probably a one-step process ... It would have been very imprudent not to have done something."
Axilrod was speaking on Reuters Financial Television.

KEVIN FLANAGAN, FIRST VICE PRESIDENT AND AN ECONOMIST, DEAN WITTER REYNOLDS INC: "It was right in line with what everyone was expecting. Everyone had pretty much factored it in. We really had kind of a rally (in the U.S. Treasury market) going into the decision, so I wouldn't be surprised if we saw a bit of profit-taking.
"The statements they made seem to keep open the possibility that they may tighten again this year," he added.

WILLIAM GRIGGS, MANAGING DIRECTOR, GRIGGS & SANTOW INC: "It was absolutely in line with expectations. They aren't concerned about the economy; they're not trying to slow the economy down. They're trying to be sure that the economy doesn't produce inflationary pressures.
"It's not aimed at the economy. It's still aimed at inflation," he added.

MARK GARGANO, MANAGING DIRECTOR, CURRENCY DERIVATIVES, FIRST UNION NATIONAL BANK: "This was the right thing to do for stability and for the dollar to stay at these levels. I suspect the crosses in Europe will be one dominant issue and economic fundamentals in the U.S. will become another dominant issue (for the dollar.) The question is now: Do they have to go all over again in May? If growth holds, it looks like they need to keep going and inflation is coming up, dollar/Europe has a chance to go up, but there's more potential in currencies outside the mark. You buy dollar/Spain, dollar/lira, dollar/Sweden, more vulnerable currencies."
GARY THAYER, SENIOR ECONOMIST, A.G. EDWARDS & SONS:

"Greenspan has basically given us a vaccination against inflation ... (The FOMC is) hoping by acting preemptively inflation won't develop, or develop that much, and it should prolong the expansion. We could see additional increases depending on commodity prices, the dollar and the rest of the world economy and how fast they start to grow. We are in a mature phase of the economic cycle and if we see further evidence of inflationary risks Greenspan has been referring to, we could see another rate increase."
JOHN WILSON, CHIEF ECONOMIST, BANK OF AMERICA: "It was a good move. The way in which it was executed was outstanding.

"The Fed fully prepared the markets ... and it is a pre-emptive strike. I think they are going to watch the economy very carefully. We are going to have two strong quarters back to back. They probably will be prepared to raise rates later in the year."
SUNG WON SOHN, CHIEF ECONOMIST, NORWEST CORP: "The economy is exceeding Greenspan's speed limit."

Sohn continued: "So I think the Fed decided to clear the beach as a precautionary move. I view this as a mid-course correction ... I don't expect this to lead to a series of tightenings as was the case in 1994.
"After all, it is anticipatory. So, I think, hopefully, we will see maybe one or two tightenings and be done with that."

DAN SETO, SENIOR ECONOMIST, THE NIKKO SECURITIES CO INTERNATIONAL INC: "With the language (Greenspan) used. (The Fed) gives me the impression that they are still on high alert. They are talking about persisting strength in the economy ... and this kind of language suggests to me that they need to see slower growth to hold them off."
